q: A limitation of the basic Economic Order Quantity model is that it assumes away certain practical features. It does NOT take into account:

options.A: The annual consumption of the material
options.B: The cost of placing an order
options.C: Quantity discounts offered by suppliers for bulk purchases

e: The basic EOQ model assumes constant consumption, ordering and carrying costs and takes the purchase price as given; it does NOT take into account quantity discounts offered for bulk purchases, which must be evaluated separately.

q: Under Emerson's efficiency (premium bonus) plan of wage payment:

options.A: Day wages are guaranteed and a bonus, which increases progressively with efficiency, begins to be payable when the worker's efficiency reaches about 66-2/3 per cent of the standard
options.B: No day wages are guaranteed to the worker at any level of efficiency
options.C: The worker is paid only on a straight piece-rate basis
options.D: Bonus is payable only when the worker exceeds 100 per cent efficiency

e: Under Emerson's efficiency plan, day wages are guaranteed and a bonus, which increases progressively with efficiency, begins to be payable when the worker's efficiency reaches about 66-2/3 per cent of the standard.

q: Under the Bedaux system of wage payment, work is measured in 'points' (B-units), where one point represents:

options.A: One unit of output produced by the worker
options.B: One hour of work done by an average worker
options.C: The quantity of work done in one hour by a worker of average skill
options.D: The amount of work, including the proper rest allowance, that can be performed in one minute

e: Under the Bedaux system, one point (B-unit) represents the amount of work, including the proper rest allowance, that can be performed in one minute; a standard hour equals 60 points.

q: Under a group bonus scheme of wage payment (such as the Priestman or Scanlon plan):

options.A: Each worker is rewarded strictly according to his own individual output
options.B: Bonus is computed on the output or savings of a group or department of workers as a whole and is shared among the members of the group
options.C: Bonus is paid only to the supervisor of the group
options.D: Bonus is paid in the form of shares of the company only

e: Under a group bonus scheme such as Priestman or Scanlon, bonus is computed on the output or savings of a group or department as a whole and is shared among the members of the group.

q: Budgeted factory overheads of a concern are Rs 90,000 and the budgeted prime cost is Rs 3,00,000. The overhead absorption rate, expressed as a percentage of prime cost, is:
e: Absorption rate as a percentage of prime cost = budgeted factory overheads / budgeted prime cost x 100 = 90,000 / 3,00,000 x 100 = 30%.

q: Budgeted factory overheads are Rs 2,50,000 and the budgeted direct labour hours are 50,000, giving an absorption rate of Rs 5 per labour hour. Actual labour hours worked are 52,000 and the actual factory overheads incurred are Rs 2,72,000. The overheads are:
e: Overheads absorbed = 52,000 hours x Rs 5 = Rs 2,60,000. Actual overheads are Rs 2,72,000, which exceed the amount absorbed, so overheads are under-absorbed by Rs 12,000.

q: Under the repeated distribution method of secondary distribution of service department overheads:

options.A: Each service department's costs are apportioned once only, in a fixed sequence
options.B: The service department with the largest cost is closed first and is never reopened
options.C: The costs of service departments are written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: The overheads of the service departments are reapportioned to one another and to the production departments again and again until the amounts remaining become negligible

e: Under the repeated distribution method, service department overheads are reapportioned to one another and to the production departments again and again until the amounts remaining in service departments become negligible.

q: The budgeted working hours of a factory are 10,000 and the actual hours worked are 9,200. The standard fixed overhead absorption rate is Rs 5 per hour. The fixed overhead capacity variance is:
e: Capacity variance = (budgeted hours - actual hours) x standard rate = (10,000 - 9,200) x Rs 5 = Rs 4,000 adverse, because fewer hours were worked than budgeted, so fixed overheads were under-recovered.

q: The total fixed overhead cost variance of a factory for a period can be analysed into:

options.A: Material price variance and material usage variance
options.B: Labour rate variance and labour efficiency variance
options.C: Fixed overhead expenditure variance and fixed overhead volume variance
options.D: Variable overhead expenditure variance and efficiency variance

e: The total fixed overhead cost variance is analysed into the fixed overhead expenditure variance (budgeted versus actual fixed overheads) and the fixed overhead volume variance (arising from output differing from the budget).

q: From the following data, the cost of goods sold is: Direct material Rs 80,000; Direct labour Rs 50,000; Direct expenses Rs 10,000; Factory overheads Rs 30,000; Office and administration overheads Rs 20,000; Opening stock of finished goods Rs 15,000; Closing stock of finished goods Rs 25,000.
e: Cost of production = prime cost 1,40,000 + factory overheads 30,000 + office overheads 20,000 = Rs 1,90,000. Cost of goods sold = 1,90,000 + opening finished stock 15,000 - closing finished stock 25,000 = Rs 1,80,000.

q: The marginal cost equation is correctly expressed as:

options.A: Sales − Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit
options.B: Sales + Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit
options.C: Sales − Fixed cost = Variable cost + Profit
options.D: Sales = Variable cost + Fixed cost − Profit

e: The marginal cost equation is Sales - Variable cost = Fixed cost + Profit, expressing that contribution (sales less variable cost) must cover the fixed costs and leave the profit.

q: A product sells for Rs 95 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 57 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 1,90,000. If 8,000 units are sold, the profit under marginal costing is:
e: Contribution = (95 - 57) x 8,000 = Rs 3,04,000. Profit = contribution - fixed costs = 3,04,000 - 1,90,000 = Rs 1,14,000, fixed costs being charged wholly to the period under marginal costing.

q: A product sells for Rs 240 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 150 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 3,60,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: Break-even point in units = fixed costs / contribution per unit = 3,60,000 / (240 - 150) = 3,60,000 / 90 = 4,000 units, at which total contribution exactly equals fixed costs.

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 2,50,000, its fixed costs are Rs 75,000 and its profit is Rs 50,000. Its P/V ratio is:
e: P/V ratio = (fixed costs + profit) / sales x 100 = (75,000 + 50,000) / 2,50,000 x 100 = 50%, since contribution equals fixed cost plus profit.

q: The fixed costs of an enterprise increase by Rs 60,000 and its P/V ratio is 40%. To maintain the same level of profit as before, the additional sales required are:
e: Additional sales required = increase in fixed costs / P/V ratio = 60,000 / 40% = Rs 1,50,000; the contribution on these extra sales exactly covers the Rs 60,000 rise in fixed costs, so profit is maintained.

q: A product sells for Rs 130 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 78 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 2,08,000. The number of units to be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 1,04,000 is:
e: Units to earn the target profit = (fixed costs + target profit) / contribution per unit = (2,08,000 + 1,04,000) / (130 - 78) = 3,12,000 / 52 = 6,000 units.

q: In a profit/volume (P/V) graph, the slope of the profit line represents:

options.A: The total fixed costs of the enterprise
options.B: The margin of safety of the enterprise
options.C: The P/V ratio of the enterprise
options.D: The break-even sales of the enterprise

e: In a P/V graph, the profit line rises by the contribution earned on each additional rupee of sales as sales increase; its slope therefore represents the P/V ratio of the enterprise.

q: Raw material is the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 150 per unit and consumes 6 kg of material per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 160 per unit and consumes 8 kg of material per unit. To maximise profit, production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per kg of material (Rs 25) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit is higher
options.C: Both products equally, as their contributions are nearly equal
options.D: Product B, because it consumes more material per unit

e: With material as the limiting factor, products are ranked by contribution per kg: A gives 150/6 = Rs 25 per kg and B gives 160/8 = Rs 20 per kg, so A gets priority despite its lower contribution per unit.

q: A factory has 14,000 kg of a scarce material. Product A, which ranks first on the basis of contribution per kg, requires 6 kg per unit and its maximum demand is 1,500 units. Product B requires 5 kg per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:
e: Material used for A's full demand = 1,500 units x 6 kg = 9,000 kg. Material remaining = 14,000 - 9,000 = 5,000 kg, giving 5,000 / 5 = 1,000 units of B.

q: A firm requires 5,000 units of a component every year. It can make the component at a variable cost of Rs 52 per unit. An outside supplier offers it at Rs 48 per unit, but buying it would involve additional fixed inspection and handling costs of Rs 24,000 per year. All other fixed costs will continue in either case. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Buy the component, as the supplier's price is lower than the variable cost of making
options.B: Make the component, as the total cost of making (Rs 2,60,000) is lower than the total cost of buying (Rs 2,64,000)
options.C: Buy the component, because fixed costs are irrelevant to the decision
options.D: Make half the quantity and buy the remaining half

e: Total cost of making = 5,000 x Rs 52 = Rs 2,60,000. Total cost of buying = (5,000 x Rs 48) + additional fixed costs 24,000 = Rs 2,64,000. Making is cheaper, so the component should be made; the other fixed costs continue either way and are irrelevant.

q: A firm is working at full capacity. Its regular selling price is Rs 100 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 60 per unit. It receives a one-time special order for 1,000 units at Rs 85 per unit, which can be executed only by displacing regular sales of 1,000 units. The special order should be:

options.A: Accepted, because the price of Rs 85 is above the variable cost of Rs 60
options.B: Accepted, because it will add a contribution of Rs 25,000
options.C: Rejected, because the contribution gained (Rs 25,000) is less than the regular contribution lost (Rs 40,000)
options.D: Accepted, because fixed costs remain unchanged

e: The special order would add contribution of 1,000 x (85 - 60) = Rs 25,000 but, at full capacity, it displaces regular sales contributing 1,000 x (100 - 60) = Rs 40,000; the net loss of Rs 15,000 means it should be rejected.

q: A division earns a contribution of Rs 1,40,000. Its specific (avoidable) fixed costs are Rs 1,10,000 and the common fixed costs allocated to it, which would continue even if the division were closed, are Rs 60,000. If the division is closed down, the total profit of the company will:

options.A: Decrease by Rs 30,000, being the segment margin forgone
options.D: Remain unchanged, as the allocated costs continue

e: Segment margin = contribution - avoidable fixed costs = 1,40,000 - 1,10,000 = Rs 30,000. Closing the division loses this margin while the Rs 60,000 common costs continue, so the total profit of the company decreases by Rs 30,000.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 4,00,000 per year, of which Rs 1,50,000 would continue to be incurred even if the plant is shut down. Shutdown (discontinuance) costs of Rs 50,000 would also be incurred on closure. The contribution is Rs 40 per unit. The shutdown point of the plant is:
e: Shutdown point = (avoidable fixed costs + shutdown costs) / contribution per unit = [(4,00,000 - 1,50,000) + 50,000] / 40 = 3,00,000 / 40 = 7,500 units; below this output, shutting down loses less than continuing.

q: A component can be made in the factory at a variable cost of Rs 64 per unit (material Rs 30, labour Rs 20 and variable overheads Rs 14). An outside supplier offers the same component at Rs 58 per unit. The fixed overheads allocated to the component will continue whether it is made or bought, and the facilities released will remain idle. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Make the component, because its total cost including fixed overheads is lower
options.B: Buy the component, saving Rs 6 per unit on the relevant cost
options.C: Make the component, because buying involves dependence on an outside supplier
options.D: Buy half the requirement and make the other half

e: Only relevant costs count: making costs Rs 64 per unit in variable cost, while buying costs Rs 58 per unit; the allocated fixed overheads continue either way and the released facilities remain idle, so buying saves Rs 6 per unit.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 20 per kg. During a period, 5,000 kg of the material are purchased at Rs 18 per kg. The material price variance, computed on the quantity purchased, is:
e: Material price variance = (standard price - actual price) x quantity purchased = (20 - 18) x 5,000 = Rs 10,000 favourable, because the material was purchased below the standard price.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour cost is 2,500 hours at Rs 35 per hour. Actual hours worked are 2,600 at Rs 38 per hour. The labour cost variance is:
e: Labour cost variance = standard cost - actual cost = (2,500 x Rs 35) - (2,600 x Rs 38) = 87,500 - 98,800 = Rs 11,300 adverse, combining the higher rate paid and the extra hours worked.

q: The actual variable overheads incurred by a factory are Rs 48,000. The actual hours worked are 6,000 and the standard variable overhead rate is Rs 7 per hour. The variable overhead expenditure variance is:
e: Variable overhead expenditure variance = actual overheads - (actual hours x standard rate) = 48,000 - (6,000 x Rs 7) = 48,000 - 42,000 = Rs 6,000 adverse; more was spent than the allowance for the hours worked.

q: In a factory, the standard production is 10 units per hour and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 4 per unit. In a period, 900 hours are actually worked and the actual output is 8,550 units. The fixed overhead efficiency variance is:
e: Standard hours for 8,550 units at 10 units per hour = 855 hours, and the standard rate is Rs 40 per hour (10 units x Rs 4). Efficiency variance = (900 - 855) x 40 = Rs 1,800 adverse.

q: In standard costing, a 'planning variance' (revision variance) arises when:

options.A: The actual performance of a department is better than the standard
options.B: A variance is caused by inefficiency in operations during the period
options.C: The original standard itself is revised during the period because of changed circumstances, so that part of the total variance is attributable to the revision of the standard
options.D: The actual output differs from the budgeted output

e: A planning (revision) variance arises when the original standard itself is revised during the period because of changed circumstances, so that part of the total variance is attributable to the revision of the standard rather than to performance.

q: Standard costing is most suitable and effective in industries where:

options.A: Production consists of standardised, repetitive operations and the output is homogeneous
options.B: Every job is executed strictly to individual customer specifications and no two jobs are alike
options.C: Production is carried on only occasionally and on a very small scale
options.D: Prices of all materials and labour change every day

e: Standard costing is most suitable where production consists of standardised, repetitive operations and the output is homogeneous, so that meaningful standards can be set and variances analysed; it is ill-suited to unique, one-off jobs.

q: In a process, 1,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 20,600. Normal loss is 10% of input and the scrap realises Rs 8 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Cost per unit of good output = (total cost - scrap value of normal loss) / expected good output = (20,600 - 100 x Rs 8) / (1,000 - 100) = 19,800 / 900 = Rs 22.00; the net cost of normal loss is borne by the good units.

q: In a process, 5,000 units are introduced and the normal loss is 5% of the input. The actual output obtained is 4,600 units. The abnormal loss is:
e: Normal loss = 5% of 5,000 = 250 units, so expected output is 4,750 units. Actual output is 4,600 units, giving an abnormal loss of 4,750 - 4,600 = 150 units.

q: Where the output of one process is transferred to the next process at a price which includes an element of profit, such a system is known as transfer at:

options.A: Market price of the finished product
options.C: Inter-process profit basis, under which a reserve is created for the unrealised profit contained in the closing stock
options.D: Cost less scrap value of normal loss

e: Transferring output to the next process at a price which includes an element of profit is the inter-process profit basis; a reserve is created for the unrealised profit contained in the closing stock.

q: A hotel incurs total operating costs of Rs 36,00,000 during a year in which the total number of room-days occupied is 12,000. The operating cost per room-day is:
e: Operating cost per room-day = total operating costs / total room-days occupied = 36,00,000 / 12,000 = Rs 300, the unit cost used in service (operating) costing for fixing charges.

q: In transport (operating) costing, which of the following is a standing charge, that is, a cost incurred whether or not the vehicles run?

options.D: Garage rent and the road licence fee of the vehicles

e: Standing charges are costs incurred whether or not the vehicles run, such as garage rent and the road licence fee; petrol, tyres and lubricants are running charges that vary with the distance run.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 10,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 3,00,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 12% is 3.605. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: PV of the annuity = 3,00,000 x 3.605 = Rs 10,81,500. NPV = 10,81,500 - 10,00,000 = (+) Rs 81,500, so the project earns more than the 12% required return and may be accepted.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 4,50,000. It is expected to yield net cash inflows of Rs 1,80,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 1,80,000 at the end of Year 2, besides a salvage value of Rs 90,000 at the end of Year 2. The present value factors at 10% are 0.909 for Year 1 and 0.826 for Year 2. The Net Present Value of the project is:
The present value of Rs 2,00,000 receivable at the end of 3 years, discounted at 10% (present value factor 0.751), is:
e: Present value = amount receivable x PV factor = 2,00,000 x 0.751 = Rs 1,50,200, the value today of Rs 2,00,000 receivable at the end of 3 years when discounted at 10%.

q: The reciprocal of the payback period (1 divided by the payback period) can be used as an approximate measure of the internal rate of return of a project when:

options.A: The project has no salvage value at the end of its life
options.B: The annual cash inflows of the project are uneven
options.C: The life of the project is shorter than its payback period
options.D: The annual cash inflows are uniform and the life of the project is considerably longer than the payback period

e: The reciprocal of the payback period approximates the IRR only when the annual cash inflows are uniform and the life of the project is considerably longer than the payback period, so that the inflows resemble a long annuity.

q: A project costing Rs 8,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 3,00,000 in Year 1, Rs 3,00,000 in Year 2 and Rs 4,00,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 3,00,000, Year 2 Rs 6,00,000. The balance Rs 2,00,000 comes from the Year 3 inflow of Rs 4,00,000, taking half a year; payback = 2 years 6 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 6,00,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 2, Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Cumulative discounted inflows: Year 1 Rs 2,00,000, Year 2 Rs 4,00,000, Year 3 Rs 5,50,000. The balance Rs 50,000 comes from the Year 4 discounted inflow of Rs 1,00,000, taking half a year; discounted payback = 3 years 6 months.

q: A project's NPV is (+) Rs 8,000 at a discount rate of 10% and (-) Rs 12,000 at a discount rate of 14%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: Interpolating between +8,000 at 10% and -12,000 at 14%: IRR = 10 + [8,000/(8,000 + 12,000)] x 4 = 10 + 1.6 = 11.6%, the rate at which NPV becomes zero.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 7,50,000 and its initial investment is Rs 6,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = PV of future cash inflows / initial investment = 7,50,000 / 6,00,000 = 1.25; since it exceeds 1, the project yields more than its cost in present value terms.

q: An investment of Rs 12,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit (after depreciation and tax) of Rs 90,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR = average annual profit after depreciation and tax / initial investment x 100 = 90,000 / 12,00,000 x 100 = 7.5%.

q: An investment of Rs 7,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 1,00,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 4,00,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 70,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: ARR on the average investment = average annual profit / average investment x 100 = 70,000 / 4,00,000 x 100 = 17.5%; the average investment of Rs 4,00,000 is the mean of the initial outlay and the salvage value over the project's life.

q: The Profitability Index of a project is also known as the:
e: The Profitability Index is the ratio of the present value of the project's benefits to its initial cost, and is therefore also known as the benefit-cost ratio; a value above 1 indicates an acceptable project.

q: In appraising a project by the Net Present Value method, using the weighted average cost of capital as the discount rate, interest on the borrowed capital employed in the project is NOT deducted separately from the project's cash flows because:

options.A: Interest is not a cost of the project at all
options.B: Interest is always paid out of the profits of earlier years
options.C: Interest is a non-cash charge like depreciation
options.D: The cost of the borrowed capital is already reflected in the discount rate, and deducting interest again would amount to double counting

e: When the WACC is used as the discount rate, the cost of borrowed capital is already reflected in that rate; deducting interest from the project's cash flows as well would amount to double counting.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 6,00,000 (cost 14%), preference capital of Rs 2,00,000 (cost 10%) and debt of Rs 4,00,000 (after-tax cost 7%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
e: WACC = (6,00,000 x 14% + 2,00,000 x 10% + 4,00,000 x 7%) / 12,00,000 = (84,000 + 20,000 + 28,000) / 12,00,000 = 11%, weighting each source's cost by its share of the total capital.

q: A company issues 8% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 80 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of debt is:
e: Cost of debt = annual interest / net proceeds = Rs 8 / Rs 80 = 10%; because the debentures are issued at a discount, the effective cost is higher than the 8% coupon rate.

q: A company issues 9% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 75 per share. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of preference capital = annual preference dividend / net proceeds = Rs 9 / Rs 75 = 12%; issue at a discount raises the effective cost above the 9% dividend rate.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 8 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 80 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 4% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = D1/P0 + g = (8/80 x 100) + 4% = 10% + 4% = 14%. The dividend yield plus the constant growth rate together give the return shareholders require.

q: The dividend growth (Gordon) model of the cost of equity capital rests on the assumption that:

options.A: The market price of the share will remain constant over time
options.B: Dividends per share will grow at a constant rate indefinitely
options.C: The company will pay out the whole of its earnings as dividend
options.D: The growth rate of dividends will exceed the cost of equity capital

e: The Gordon model assumes dividends per share grow at one constant rate forever, which lets the infinite stream of future dividends be valued as D1/(Ke - g). Constant growth is its core assumption.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 7%, the expected market return is 15% and the beta of the share is 0.75, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf) = 7% + 0.75 x (15% - 7%) = 7% + 6% = 13%. CAPM adds the market risk premium, scaled by beta, to the risk-free rate.

q: Under the Modigliani-Miller hypothesis WITH corporate taxes, the value of a firm increases with the use of debt mainly because:

options.A: Interest on debt is a tax-deductible expense, so debt creates an interest tax shield
options.B: The cost of equity falls as the proportion of debt increases
options.C: Dividends paid by a levered firm become exempt from tax
options.D: The business risk of the firm decreases with borrowing

e: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so borrowing creates an interest tax shield that reduces the firm's tax bill. Under MM with corporate taxes, this shield raises the value of the levered firm.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000, variable costs are Rs 10,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 4,50,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Contribution = Rs 16,00,000 - Rs 10,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000; EBIT = Rs 6,00,000 - Rs 4,50,000 = Rs 1,50,000. Degree of operating leverage = Contribution/EBIT = 6,00,000/1,50,000 = 4.0.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 9,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 6,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT/(EBIT - Interest) = Rs 9,00,000/(Rs 9,00,000 - Rs 6,00,000) = 9,00,000/3,00,000 = 3.0.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 22,00,000, variable costs of Rs 12,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 5,00,000 and interest of Rs 3,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Contribution = Rs 22,00,000 - Rs 12,00,000 = Rs 10,00,000; EBT = Rs 10,00,000 - Rs 5,00,000 - Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 2,00,000. Degree of combined leverage = Contribution/EBT = 10,00,000/2,00,000 = 5.0.

q: The degree of operating leverage of an enterprise is 2.5. If its sales increase by 20%, its earnings before interest and tax will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage change in EBIT = DOL x percentage change in sales = 2.5 x 20% = 50%. Operating leverage magnifies the effect of a sales change on operating profit.

q: The operating (business) risk of an enterprise arises mainly from:

options.A: The use of borrowed capital in its capital structure
options.B: Changes in the rate of income tax
options.C: Fluctuations in the market price of its shares
options.D: The presence of fixed operating costs, which causes wide fluctuations in operating profit (EBIT) with changes in sales

e: Operating (business) risk comes from fixed operating costs in the cost structure: because these costs do not fall with sales, EBIT fluctuates widely when sales change. Borrowing creates financial risk, not operating risk.

q: The financial break-even point of an enterprise is the level of earnings before interest and tax at which:

options.A: The net present value of the enterprise is zero
options.B: The earnings per share is zero
options.C: The total contribution is exactly equal to the fixed operating costs
options.D: The degree of financial leverage is exactly one

e: The financial break-even point is the EBIT level at which earnings per share is exactly zero, i.e. EBIT just covers interest and preference dividend, leaving nothing for equity shareholders.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 11,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 5,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets/Current liabilities = Rs 11,00,000/Rs 5,00,000 = 2.2 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 14,00,000, including stock of Rs 5,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 1,00,000. Current liabilities are Rs 5,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = Rs 14,00,000 - stock Rs 5,00,000 - prepaid expenses Rs 1,00,000 = Rs 8,00,000 (stock and prepaid expenses are not quickly realisable). Quick ratio = 8,00,000/5,00,000 = 1.6 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 14,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 10,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt/Shareholders' funds = Rs 14,00,000/Rs 10,00,000 = 1.4 : 1.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 1,10,000 on sales of Rs 10,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = Net profit/Sales x 100 = Rs 1,10,000/Rs 10,00,000 x 100 = 11%.

q: A very high inventory turnover ratio in an enterprise may, besides indicating efficient inventory management, also indicate:

options.C: Under-stocking, with the risk of stock-outs and loss of sales
options.D: A large proportion of slow-moving items in stock

e: A very high inventory turnover may mean the firm keeps too little stock: frequent stock-outs, interrupted production and lost sales, even though it can also reflect efficient inventory management.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 21,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 3,00,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = Credit sales/Average debtors = Rs 21,00,000/Rs 3,00,000 = 7 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 29,20,000 and its average debtors are Rs 2,00,000. Taking a year of 365 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = 365/Debtors turnover = 365 x Rs 2,00,000/Rs 29,20,000 = 25 days.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 8,50,000 and the interest payable is Rs 1,70,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = PBIT/Interest = Rs 8,50,000/Rs 1,70,000 = 5 times. It shows how many times the operating profit covers the interest obligation.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 5,50,000 and its capital employed is Rs 11,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: Return on Capital Employed = PBIT/Capital employed x 100 = Rs 5,50,000/Rs 11,00,000 x 100 = 50%.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 6,40,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 80,000. If the company has 70,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (Net profit after tax - Preference dividend)/Number of equity shares = (Rs 6,40,000 - Rs 80,000)/70,000 = Rs 5,60,000/70,000 = Rs 8.00.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 90 and its Earnings Per Share is Rs 6. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
e: P/E ratio = Market price per share/EPS = Rs 90/Rs 6 = 15. It shows the price investors pay for each rupee of current earnings.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 5,50,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 90,000 and a loss of Rs 15,000 on the sale of plant, and after crediting a profit of Rs 45,000 on the sale of investments. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = Rs 5,50,000 + depreciation Rs 90,000 + loss on sale of plant Rs 15,000 - profit on sale of investments Rs 45,000 = Rs 6,10,000. Non-cash and non-operating items are adjusted back.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 4,20,000. During the year, its stock increased by Rs 55,000, its debtors decreased by Rs 35,000 and its creditors increased by Rs 15,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = Rs 4,20,000 - stock increase Rs 55,000 + debtors decrease Rs 35,000 + creditors increase Rs 15,000 = Rs 4,15,000. Increases in current assets consume cash; increases in current liabilities release it.

q: During a year, the current assets of an enterprise decreased by Rs 80,000 and its current liabilities decreased by Rs 30,000. The net change in its working capital is:
e: Change in working capital = change in current assets - change in current liabilities = (-Rs 80,000) - (-Rs 30,000) = -Rs 50,000, i.e. a decrease of Rs 50,000.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the repayment of a long-term bank loan is classified as:

options.C: It is not shown in the cash flow statement

e: Repayment of a long-term bank loan is a financing activity under AS-3, because it changes the size and composition of the borrowings of the enterprise; it is neither operating nor investing.

q: A fund flow statement is popularly described as a statement of:

options.A: Cash receipts and cash payments during a period
options.B: 'Where got and where gone' - the sources from which funds were obtained and the uses to which they were put
options.C: Assets and liabilities at a point of time
options.D: Income and expenditure of a period

e: A fund flow statement shows where funds came from and where they went during a period - the sources of funds and their applications - which is why it is called a 'where got and where gone' statement.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 7,200 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 90,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = Net earnings/Capital-at-charge x 100 = Rs 7,200 crore/Rs 90,000 crore x 100 = 8%.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 3,00,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 2,76,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = Ordinary working expenses/Gross traffic receipts x 100 = Rs 2,76,000 crore/Rs 3,00,000 crore x 100 = 92%. A lower ratio means more surplus left from traffic earnings.

q: A proposed railway work is estimated to cost Rs 500 crore and is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 65 crore after meeting the additional working expenses. The anticipated rate of return on the work, and its financial status, are:

options.B: 10%; the work just meets the prescribed test
options.D: 13%; the work is remunerative, as it exceeds the prescribed 10% test

e: Rate of return = Rs 65 crore/Rs 500 crore x 100 = 13%. Since 13% exceeds the prescribed 10% test of financial justification, the work is remunerative.

q: Consequent upon the merger of the Railway Budget with the General Budget with effect from 2017-18, the payment of dividend by Indian Railways to General Revenues on its capital-at-charge was:

options.A: Raised to a flat rate of 6%
options.C: Continued at the rate recommended by the Railway Convention Committee
options.D: Transferred to the Railway Safety Fund

e: After the Railway Budget merged with the General Budget from 2017-18, Indian Railways stopped paying dividend to General Revenues on capital-at-charge; the payment was discontinued.

q: The 'budget period' in most business enterprises is normally:

options.A: One month only, in all cases
options.B: One financial year, subdivided into shorter periods such as months or quarters for the purpose of control
options.D: An indefinite period, fixed only when the budget is actually prepared

e: The budget period is normally one financial year, broken into shorter periods such as months or quarters so that actual performance can be compared with the budget regularly for control.

q: A sales budget provides for the sale of 25,000 units of a product at a budgeted selling price of Rs 40 per unit. The budgeted sales value is:
e: Budgeted sales value = 25,000 units x Rs 40 per unit = Rs 10,00,000.

q: A factory's finished-goods production budget for a period is 30,000 units. The opening work-in-progress is equivalent to 2,000 finished units and the closing work-in-progress is to be equivalent to 3,000 finished units. The number of units to be put into production is:
e: Units to put into production = production required + closing WIP - opening WIP = 30,000 + 3,000 - 2,000 = 31,000 units, expressed in finished-unit equivalents.

q: Production of 15,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 2.5 kg of material. The opening stock of material is 5,500 kg and the closing stock is to be 7,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material required = 15,000 units x 2.5 kg = 37,500 kg. Purchases = requirement + closing stock - opening stock = 37,500 + 7,000 - 5,500 = 39,000 kg.

q: A cash budget shows an opening cash balance of Rs 15,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,40,000 and estimated payments of Rs 2,35,000 for a month. The closing cash balance will be:
e: Closing cash balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = Rs 15,000 + Rs 2,40,000 - Rs 2,35,000 = Rs 20,000.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 1,80,000 and variable costs of Rs 9 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 14,000 units is:
e: Flexed budget = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x actual output) = Rs 1,80,000 + (Rs 9 x 14,000) = Rs 1,80,000 + Rs 1,26,000 = Rs 3,06,000.

q: In a large organisation, the 'Budget Officer' (Budget Director) is the executive who:

options.A: Sanctions all the expenditure of the enterprise
options.B: Conducts the statutory audit of the enterprise
options.C: Coordinates budget preparation — issuing the timetable and instructions, collecting and consolidating the functional budgets and reporting performance against the budgets
options.D: Fixes the selling prices of the products of the enterprise

e: The Budget Officer (Budget Director) coordinates the whole budgeting exercise - issuing the timetable and instructions, collecting and consolidating the functional budgets, and reporting performance against budget. He does not sanction expenditure or audit.

q: Under zero-base budgeting, besides the minimum (survival) package for an activity, a manager may prepare one or more 'incremental packages' which show:

options.A: The budget of the previous year restated at current prices
options.B: A list of the staff of the activity proposed to be retrenched
options.C: The fixed assets required by the activity during the year
options.D: The additional cost and the additional benefit of progressively higher levels of funding and performance for the same activity, so that management can choose the level to be funded

e: In zero-base budgeting, incremental packages show the extra cost and extra benefit of funding an activity at progressively higher levels above the minimum survival package, so management can choose the level to fund.

q: Performance budgeting was first introduced in the Government of India following the recommendations of the:
e: Performance budgeting - linking outlays to physical outputs and programmes - was introduced in the Government of India following the recommendations of the Administrative Reforms Commission.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 50 days, the production process takes 15 days, finished goods are held for 10 days and debtors take 45 days to pay. Suppliers allow 30 days' credit. The length of the operating (cash conversion) cycle is:
e: Operating cycle = raw material holding 50 + production 15 + finished goods holding 10 + debtors collection 45 - creditors credit 30 = 90 days.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 54,00,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 80 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = annual operating cost x operating cycle/360 = Rs 54,00,000 x 80/360 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 16,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 6,50,000. Its net working capital is:
e: Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = Rs 16,00,000 - Rs 6,50,000 = Rs 9,50,000.

q: Public utility undertakings (such as water supply and electricity undertakings) generally require comparatively small working capital mainly because:

options.A: They have no customers to supply
options.B: Their services are sold largely for cash and the demand for them is continuous and steady, so that little funds are locked up in stocks of finished goods or in debtors
options.C: They are financed entirely out of government grants
options.D: They do not purchase any raw materials or stores

e: Public utilities sell services largely for cash and face continuous, steady demand, so little capital is locked up in finished-goods stock or debtors; hence their working capital needs are comparatively small.

q: The fundamental trade-off in working capital management is between:

options.A: Liquidity and profitability — larger current assets increase liquidity and reduce risk but lower profitability, while smaller current assets do the reverse

e: Working capital management trades liquidity against profitability: more current assets mean greater liquidity and safety but lower returns, while leaner current assets raise profitability at the cost of higher risk.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 600 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 5 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = maximum consumption x maximum re-order period = 600 units x 5 weeks = 3,000 units. Ordering at this level ensures stock lasts until fresh supplies arrive, even in the worst case.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,600 units. Normal consumption is 180 units per week and the normal re-order period is 7 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum level = Re-order level - (normal consumption x normal re-order period) = 2,600 - (180 x 7) = 2,600 - 1,260 = 1,340 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,400 units and the re-order quantity is 2,200 units. Minimum consumption is 80 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 4 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum level = Re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum re-order period) = 3,400 + 2,200 - (80 x 4) = 5,600 - 320 = 5,280 units.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 500 units per week, the normal consumption is 350 units per week and the maximum lead time is 6 weeks. The safety stock, computed as (Maximum consumption − Normal consumption) × Maximum lead time, is:
e: Safety stock = (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time = (500 - 350) x 6 = 150 x 6 = 900 units, held to guard against abnormal usage and delay.

q: The maximum stock level of a material is 4,600 units and the minimum stock level is 1,400 units. The average stock level, computed as (Maximum level + Minimum level) ÷ 2, is:
e: Average stock level = (Maximum level + Minimum level)/2 = (4,600 + 1,400)/2 = 3,000 units.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 4,900 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 40 and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C) = sqrt(2 x 4,900 x 40/5) = sqrt(78,400) = 280 units, the quantity at which ordering cost and carrying cost together are minimum.
